questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute the horizontal range of a projectile
questions.stem: A ball is launched horizontally at 10 m/s from a height of 5 m. How far does it travel horizontally before hitting the ground? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Time to fall: h = half g t squared, so t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(10/9.8) = 1.01 s. Horizontal distance = v t = 10 times 1.01 = 10.1 m. Using the launch speed for the vertical motion, or forgetting the square root, both give wrong times.
questions.hint: Find the fall time first, then multiply by horizontal speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: An object is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. How far does it fall in the first 1.5 s? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Distance fallen from rest: d = 0.5*g*t^2 = 0.5*9.8*2.25 = 11.025 m. Since the total fall time is about 2.02 s, the object has not hit the ground yet, so 11.0 m is valid.
questions.hint: Use d = one-half g t squared for motion starting from rest.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: apply the kinematic equation for displacement
questions.stem: Which kinematic equation relates displacement, initial velocity, acceleration, and time without using final velocity?

options.misconception: thinks the velocity equation avoids final velocity
thinks the v-squared equation has final velocity
thinks the average-velocity equation omits final velocity

questions.explanation: The equation x = x0 + v0 t + 0.5 a t^2 includes displacement, initial velocity, acceleration, and time but not final velocity. Option A has final velocity. Option C has final velocity and no time. Option D needs final velocity.
questions.hint: Look for the equation that contains t but not v (final).

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: On a position versus time graph, what does the slope at a point represent?

options.misconception: thinks the position-time slope gives acceleration
thinks the position-time slope is the displacement
thinks the position-time slope gives distance traveled

questions.explanation: The slope of a position-time graph equals instantaneous velocity. Acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph. Displacement is the vertical axis value difference, and distance traveled is total path length.
questions.hint: Slope = rise over run = change in position over change in time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: identify independence of horizontal and vertical motion
questions.stem: In projectile motion (ignoring air resistance), which statement is true about the horizontal and vertical components?

options.misconception: confuses the correct concept with a related but wrong belief
confuses the correct concept with a related but wrong belief

options.text: Both motions have the same acceleration
options.misconception: confuses the correct concept with a related but wrong belief

questions.explanation: Projectile motion separates into independent horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration due to gravity) components. Neither affects the other. Their accelerations differ: horizontal acceleration is zero, vertical is g.
questions.hint: Think about whether throwing a ball harder horizontally changes how fast it falls.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute final velocity after free fall
questions.stem: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its speed after falling for 2.0 s? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: For free fall from rest, v = g t = 9.8 * 2.0 = 19.6 m/s. Using v = d/t with d = 0.5*g*t^2 gives the same result, but averaging speeds incorrectly would not.
questions.hint: Velocity under constant acceleration from rest is g times time.

questions.learningObjective: compute time of flight for a symmetric projectile
questions.stem: A projectile is launched horizontally from a cliff 19.6 m high. How long until it hits the ground? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Vertical motion: h = 0.5 g t^2, so t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(39.2/9.8) = sqrt(4) = 2.0 s. Horizontal speed does not affect fall time.
questions.hint: Ignore horizontal speed; solve vertical free-fall time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: A car drives 100 m east, then 100 m west, returning to its start. What is its displacement?

options.misconception: thinks displacement equals the total distance traveled
thinks displacement keeps the direction of the first leg
thinks displacement adds the legs with the last direction

questions.explanation: Displacement is final position minus initial position; returning to the start gives zero displacement. Distance traveled is 200 m. Speed/velocity magnitude differs from displacement.
questions.hint: Displacement depends only on start and end points.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: On a velocity versus time graph, what does the area under the curve represent?

options.misconception: thinks the area under a v-t graph gives acceleration
thinks the area under a v-t graph gives speed
thinks the area under a v-t graph gives force

questions.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement (change in position). Acceleration is the slope, not the area. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, and force is unrelated without mass.
questions.hint: Area = velocity times time = displacement.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute maximum height of a projectile
questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight upward with initial speed 15 m/s. What is its maximum height? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: At max height v = 0, so v^2 = v0^2 - 2 g h gives h = v0^2/(2g) = 225/(19.6) = 11.48 m. Using h = v0*t with t = v0/g overcounts because speed decreases.
questions.hint: Set final velocity to zero and solve for height.

questions.learningObjective: compare fall times for different masses
questions.stem: Two objects of different masses are dropped from the same height in a vacuum. Which hits the ground first?

options.text: The heavier object always hits first
options.misconception: confuses the correct concept with a related but wrong belief

options.text: The lighter object always hits first
options.misconception: confuses the correct concept with a related but wrong belief
confuses the correct concept with a related but wrong belief

options.text: They hit at the same time

questions.explanation: In a vacuum all objects fall with acceleration g regardless of mass, so they hit simultaneously. Heavier-first and shape-dependence are air-resistance misconceptions; in vacuum shape does not matter.
questions.hint: Air resistance is absent; only gravity acts.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: A runner covers 400 m in 50 s. What is the average speed in m/s? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance / total time = 400/50 = 8.0 m/s. Average velocity would require displacement; here distance is given, so speed is the right quantity.
questions.hint: Divide total distance by total time.

questions.learningObjective: relate constant velocity to graph shape
questions.stem: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph indicates the object is...

options.misconception: thinks a horizontal v-t line means the object is at rest
thinks a horizontal v-t line means uniform acceleration
thinks a horizontal v-t line means slowing to a stop

questions.explanation: A horizontal line on v-t means velocity is constant (unchanging). At rest would be a line at v = 0. Uniform acceleration is a sloped straight line. Deceleration to rest is a line sloping to zero.
questions.hint: Horizontal means zero slope, hence zero acceleration.

questions.learningObjective: compute horizontal component of launch velocity
questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 25 m/s at 30 degrees above horizontal. What is its horizontal velocity component? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Horizontal component = v cos(theta) = 25 * cos(30°) = 25 * 0.866 = 21.65 m/s. Using sin instead gives the vertical component. Horizontal velocity stays constant (ignoring air resistance).
questions.hint: Use cosine for the horizontal component.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration in m/s^2? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: a = (v - v0)/t = (25 - 5)/4 = 5.0 m/s^2. Dividing final velocity by time (25/4) ignores initial velocity and gives a wrong acceleration.
questions.hint: Acceleration is change in velocity over time.

questions.stem: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, which launch angle gives maximum horizontal range (ignoring air resistance)?

options.misconception: thinks 30 degrees gives the maximum range on level ground

questions.explanation: Maximum range on level ground occurs at 45 degrees, balancing horizontal and vertical components. 90 degrees gives max height but zero range; 30 and 60 give equal (shorter) ranges.

questions.stem: An object starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 3 m/s^2 for 4 s. What is its displacement in meters? Report the number only.

questions.learningObjective: identify motion from position-time graph shape
questions.stem: A straight line with negative slope on a position-time graph means the object is...

options.misconception: thinks a sloped position-time line means accelerating

options.text: At rest at a negative position
options.misconception: thinks a negative slope means the object sits still
thinks a negative slope means the object slows down

questions.explanation: A straight line (constant slope) on x-t means constant velocity; negative slope means negative velocity. Curvature would indicate acceleration. At rest is zero slope; slowing down is a slope approaching zero.
questions.hint: Straight line means constant velocity; sign of slope gives direction.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 45 degrees on level ground. What is its horizontal range? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Range = v^2 sin(2 theta)/g = 400 * sin(90°)/9.8 = 400/9.8 = 40.82 m. Using R = v^2/g without sin(2 theta) overcounts for non-45° angles but happens to match here only by coincidence.
questions.hint: Use R = v^2 sin(2 theta) / g.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: How far does a freely falling object travel during its 3rd second of fall? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Distance in nth second = g(n - 0.5) = 9.8 * 2.5 = 24.5 m. Equivalently d(3)-d(2) = 0.5*9.8*9 - 0.5*9.8*4 = 44.1 - 19.6 = 24.5 m. Using 0.5*g*3^2 gives total distance, not the interval.
questions.hint: Subtract distance at end of 2nd second from distance at end of 3rd second.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.stem: An object moving with constant velocity has acceleration equal to...

options.misconception: thinks constant velocity still means free fall at g
thinks acceleration equals velocity divided by time
thinks speed squared over radius is the acceleration

questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no change in velocity, so acceleration is zero. g applies only to free fall. v/t is not a standard formula here, and v^2/r is centripetal acceleration for circular motion.
questions.hint: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
